content: Each line of a screen appears in turn. A bare string is a line of text. Long lines wrap at word boundaries to fit the window, so try resizing it.

Click anywhere, or press <esc>, to skip to the end of a screen. This program sets "waitForReveal": true, so links and other controls only work once their screen has finished revealing, as on a real terminal: until then, clicking one skips ahead too.
Scanlines are on by default. "effects" in the config turns effects on or off and tunes them, and each screen can override that. Each of these screens turns one on:
Phosphor afterglow is a screen transition: the old screen fades out behind the new one.
A static transition flashes noise between screens, like changing channels:
A screen can be nothing but effects, and "next" moves on without a link:
This screen sets "transition": "static": a 120ms burst of noise before it appears. Set a "duration" to change it.
The static screen had no content and "next": { "after": 1500, ... }.
This one has "next": { "key": "any", ... }. Press any key or click to continue.
Analog TV noise. Options: opacity, fps, scale.
Bright text and images glow into the dark around them. Options: strength, radius.
The corners of the screen darken, like the edge of a tube. Option: strength.
The picture dims by small, irregular amounts. Option: strength.
Red and cyan fringes on the text, like misaligned color guns. Options: offset, strength.
This screen turns the scanlines off.
This screen sets "transition": { "type": "fade", "duration": 1500 }, so the screen you came from faded out slowly behind it.
Links and commands can open dialogs. An alert closes with <enter>, <esc> or a click:
A confirm dialog asks a question, and each answer can do something:
A bar runs from one value to another over a set time, then the screen carries on. It can run backwards, and hide its value:
Or do something when it's done. This one uploads, and you can abort it with <esc>:
UPLOADING STATION LOGS. PRESS <ESC> TO ABORT.

When a screen is taller than the window, it scrolls to keep the newest text in view. Scroll up to reread and it stops following; scroll back down and it picks up again. Set "autoscroll": false in the config or on a screen to turn it off.
This screen sets "autoscroll": false, so the window stays where it is while the log types in below the fold. Scroll down yourself to follow it.
Drag a slider, or focus it with <tab> and use the arrow keys. It remembers its value, and can do something when the value enters a range.
Tune the receiver to find a hidden transmission (somewhere above 100):
Push the reactor past 80% and it turns red; past 95% sounds the alarm. Or press <enter> on it to confirm a setting:
THIS IS MINING STATION YPSILON-14. IF YOU CAN HEAR THIS, DO NOT DOCK. REPEAT: DO NOT DOCK.
A program can keep variables, declared in its config. Actions set them, controls can be bound to them, "if" tests them, and text shows them: hello, {name}. You have {credits} credits.
It's empty, {name}. Someone got here first.
A program can have its own sound effects, and play them wherever it likes. This screen played one as it appeared.

content.text: This line plays one as it starts to appear.

content: Links play one as they're followed:
Design your own on the sound test page (?sound, Custom tab).
A screen's "next" can list rules, and the first to trigger wins. This one has three: Y, N (or Esc), and a 10 second timeout.

A section is a header that expands and collapses the elements under it. Click one, or focus it with <tab> and press <enter>. They remember whether they're open. These set "indent": 4, so their contents sit four columns in.

content.title: SEALED CONTAINER
content: Sections can hold sections. This one sets "reveal": "glitch".

content.title: STATION STATUS
content: This one sets "open": true, so it starts expanded, and its contents reveal before the rest of the screen.

A header and a status bar are lines pinned to the top and bottom of the window. They don't scroll or reveal, and they stay put between screens: set "header" and "footer" in the config for every screen, or on a screen, like this one, for just that screen (or false to hide them).
A line is text, or "left", "center" and "right" spread across it. They can show variables, which update as they change, and hold links, like [?] HELP below.
A "pause" element stops the reveal and waits for a key or a tap, so a long screen can be read a page at a time.
STATION LOG, DAY 38. Routine maintenance on the lower deck. Mbeki reports the sensors are clean.
STATION LOG, DAY 39. Night shift heard knocking in the service ducts. Probably thermal contraction.
STATION LOG, DAY 40. The knocking has a pattern. Three, then two, then three.
Skipping stops at each pause too. Its text can be changed, and centered, like the [ MORE ] above.
A row of buttons, each only as wide as its label. Click one, tab to it and press <enter>, or press its hotkey (the underlined letter) from anywhere on the screen. The arrow keys move along the row.
A number input is a prompt that only takes whole numbers. It can limit the digits, hide them for a code, check a range, and keep the number in a variable.
The vault door takes a four-digit code (try 1138):
Set the fuel mix, from 0 to 100 (it's {fuel} now):

A program's timers keep running from screen to screen. Actions start, stop and reset them, text and bars show them by name in braces (this one's is ticking in the status bar), and when one runs out, its action happens wherever the player is. Arm this one and go somewhere else, if you dare.
A timer element can also run a timer of its own, which starts when it appears and stops when you leave:
The station is gone. That's what a program timer's onComplete can do, wherever you were.
A meter is a gauge: a bar showing a number variable or a timer, which moves whenever the value does. The player can't change it directly; actions and sliders can.
A slider and a meter can share a variable: one to set it, one to show it.
A table lays rows and columns out in character columns, each as wide as its widest cell. Columns can be aligned left, right or center; cells can show variables.
Without a box, its columns are simply spaced apart:
A menu is a list of choices, like a BIOS or DOS menu. Move the highlight with <up> and <down> (or the mouse), and choose with <enter> (or a click). Each item can also have a hotkey: here, its number.
An image's "reveal" picks how it appears, with an optional "duration": { "type": "raster", "duration": 3000 }. They run one after another; choose > AGAIN to watch them again.

content: Text can come from a file, with "src": paste ASCII art into a .txt file, no escaping needed, and it's shown exactly. Like all text, it types out:
A preset is a ready-made screen, set up with "preset": { "type": ... } and a few settings instead of content. Every line of text has a default and can be changed, or left out with false.
Each one is ordinary content underneath (text, checklists, counters, pauses), so anything a preset does can be written out by hand too.
Starts up, then waits for a key: browsers only play sound once you've pressed one.
Every line changed, and a check that fails.
Shuts down, then switches the screen off. Press a key to switch it back on.
A fatal error in a blinking box. Press a key to restart.
Garbage that never stops. Press a key to restart.
A checklist's lines appear one at a time, each followed after a moment by its status:
Lines can have their own status, and the gap can be blank. This one waits longer, and ends 40 characters in:
A counter counts quickly to its number, then adds its "done" text, like a memory test:
It can count down from a number, and take its time. This one is in the alert color:
And it can count in steps, here of 256:
Line art that moves, sized in characters and lines, and drawn in the screen's colors. Pure decoration: it goes on until you leave.
"waveform": an oscilloscope trace. A sine wave, then a sine, square and noise added together:
"chart": telemetry scrolling past, as a line or as bars (these in the alert color):
"radar": a sweep, with blips that flare as it passes:
"wireframe": a turning shape. A cube, an icosahedron and a torus:
A toggle cycles through its states each time you click it. Toggles remember their state, so leave this screen and come back.
A choice shows all its options at once. Click one, or tab to it and use the arrow keys. This one keeps its choice in a variable:
And this one has its own markers:
With "multiple": true, any number of options can be ticked, like checkboxes:
With just one option, it's a single checkbox:
Type a command and press <enter>. Commands ignore case and extra spaces. Try:

By default, text teletypes in at 10ms per character.

content: Screens and the config can set defaults too: the next screen shows everything instantly.
This screen sets "reveal": "instant", so its elements appear at once. No typing, no glitching: every line is simply there, the moment the screen opens.
That makes it handy for screens the reader will come back to often, such as menus, maps and status readouts, where waiting for the text to type out again would get tiresome.
It's also good for long reference text, like a manual page or a crew roster, which is better read at the reader's own pace than watched as it appears.
All of this arrived in a single frame...
